adjudication_records.issue_text: src/sentry/spans/buffer.py:197 — Switching live span keys from SET to ZSET makes rolling deploys and rollbacks fail with WRONGTYPE until every in-flight key expires

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows a change from Redis SET operations (sadd, scard, sscan, sunionstore) to ZSET operations (zadd, zcard, zscan, zunionstore) for the same keys (span-buf:s:{project_and_trace}:{span_id}). During a rolling deployment, old instances will use SET commands while new instances use ZSET commands on the same keys. Redis will return WRONGTYPE errors when a SET command is executed on a ZSET key or vice versa. This is a real deployment issue that would cause failures until all keys expire or all instances are updated.

adjudication_records.issue_text: src/sentry/spans/buffer.py:197 — Insertion and eviction run in separate non-transactional pipelines, so a crash or concurrent flush can leave or emit an uncapped segment after the load-time count guard was removed

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows that in buffer.py, the max_segment_spans check was removed from _load_segment_data (lines 446-452 deleted). The Lua script add-buffer.lua now enforces a 1000 span limit via zpopmin, but this happens during insertion. The finding correctly identifies that the Python code's zadd in process_spans (line 196-198) and the Lua script's eviction run in separate operations. If a crash occurs between insertion and the Lua script's zpopmin, or during concurrent flushes, segments could exceed the intended limit since the load-time guard was removed. This is a valid race condition concern.

adjudication_records.issue_text: src/sentry/scripts/spans/add-buffer.lua:47 — ZUNIONSTORE defaults to SUM, so replayed payloads present in both sets acquire inflated timestamps and can evict genuinely newer spans

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows ZUNIONSTORE being used at lines 47-48 and 52-53 in add-buffer.lua. ZUNIONSTORE by default uses SUM aggregation for scores when the same member exists in multiple sets. The scores are end_timestamp_precise values (as shown in buffer.py line 196-198 where zadd uses span.end_timestamp_precise as the score). If a span payload appears in both sets being merged (e.g., due to replay/reprocessing), its score would be doubled, making it appear newer than it actually is. This could cause the zpopmin at line 60 to evict genuinely newer spans instead of older ones when enforcing the 1000 span limit.

adjudication_records.issue_text: src/sentry/scripts/spans/add-buffer.lua:30 — Lowering redirect traversal to 1000 silently splits deeper or adversarial traces at an intermediate parent instead of the actual segment root

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows the loop limit being reduced from 10000 to 1000 at line 30. The original comment stated 'theoretically this limit means that segment trees of depth 10k may not be joined together correctly.' By reducing this to 1000, traces with redirect chains deeper than 1000 will now be silently truncated at an intermediate parent rather than reaching the actual segment root. This is a real architectural concern - the change trades off correctness for performance without clear documentation of the new limitation. However, this is not strictly a bug since the original code also had a limit (just higher), and very deep traces are likely edge cases. It's an important design decision that could affect trace integrity in certain scenarios.

adjudication_records.issue_text: tests/sentry/spans/test_buffer.py:126 — The tests only retrofit timestamps and never exceed the 1000-span boundary, leaving eviction selection and enforcement completely unverified

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows new eviction logic in add-buffer.lua (lines checking if span_count > 1000 and calling zpopmin to remove excess spans), but examining the test file changes, all tests only add small numbers of spans (4-6 spans per test) with retrofitted end_timestamp_precise values. No test creates more than 1000 spans to verify the eviction boundary works correctly. This is a legitimate test coverage gap for newly added nontrivial logic - the eviction feature is completely untested.

adjudication_records.issue_text: src/sentry/spans/buffer.py:197 — Reusing existing span-buffer keys as sorted sets without a versioned migration makes pre-deploy SET data trigger Redis WRONGTYPE failures during rollout.

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows that in buffer.py line 197, the code changes from using `p.sadd(set_key, ...)` (Redis SET operations) to `p.zadd(set_key, ...)` (Redis SORTED SET operations). The key format `span-buf:s:{project_and_trace}:{parent_span_id}` remains the same. Similarly, the Lua script in add-buffer.lua changes from `scard`/`sunionstore` to `zcard`/`zunionstore`. During a rolling deployment, if old data exists in Redis as SET type and new code tries to use ZADD/ZCARD on those keys, Redis will return WRONGTYPE errors because you cannot use sorted set commands on a set data type. The finding correctly identifies this migration issue.

adjudication_records.issue_text: src/sentry/scripts/spans/add-buffer.lua:62 — Hard-coding the eviction limit to 1000 ignores the public SpansBuffer.max_segment_spans setting, so callers can no longer configure this boundary.

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows that in add-buffer.lua, the eviction limit is hard-coded to 1000 (line 62: `if span_count > 1000 then redis.call("zpopmin", set_key, span_count - 1000)`). Looking at buffer.py, there is a `max_segment_spans` attribute on SpansBuffer class (referenced in the removed code at lines 446-452 where it was used for validation). The Lua script now enforces a fixed 1000 limit that cannot be configured through the Python SpansBuffer.max_segment_spans setting, creating an inconsistency where the Python configuration is ignored by the Redis-side enforcement.

adjudication_records.issue_text: src/sentry/api/endpoints/organization_auditlogs.py:79 — Selecting OptimizedCursorPaginator for a datetime ordering makes any nonempty optimized audit-log request raise TypeError when the paginator calls math.floor on a datetime.

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key() calls math.floor/math.ceil on the value obtained from getattr(item, self.key). When used with order_by='-datetime' for audit logs, self.key would be 'datetime', meaning it would call math.floor on a datetime object, which would raise TypeError. The DateTimePaginator (the original paginator) likely has proper handling for datetime values, but OptimizedCursorPaginator inherits from BasePaginator and uses numeric math operations that are incompatible with datetime objects.

adjudication_records.issue_text: src/sentry/api/paginator.py:880 — The advertised negative-offset cursor path passes a negative slice to Django QuerySet, which rejects negative indexing and returns a server error instead of a page.

src/sentry/api/endpoints/organization_auditlogs.py:70 — Reading optimized_pagination outside AuditLogQueryParamSerializer leaves the new public query parameter untyped and silently treats invalid values as false.

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows that `request.GET.get("optimized_pagination")` is read directly on line 70 without going through the existing `AuditLogQueryParamSerializer` that validates other query parameters (event, actor_id). This is a valid architectural concern - the new query parameter bypasses the established validation pattern, leaving it untyped and undocumented in the API schema. While not a bug per se (the code will work), it's a legitimate code review issue about consistency and API design.

adjudication_records.issue_text: src/sentry/api/paginator.py:840 — OptimizedCursorPaginator applies floor/ceil to the audit log datetime key, causing an unhandled TypeError whenever the first page contains results.

adjudication.rationale: The OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key method at line 840 uses math.floor/math.ceil on the value obtained from getattr(item, self.key). When used with audit logs ordered by '-datetime', the key would be 'datetime' and the value would be a datetime object. Calling math.floor() or math.ceil() on a datetime object raises TypeError because datetime objects don't support these operations. The DateTimePaginator handles this correctly by converting to timestamp first, but OptimizedCursorPaginator doesn't.

adjudication_records.issue_text: src/sentry/api/paginator.py:882 — The advanced negative-offset path passes a negative slice boundary to a Django QuerySet, causing an unhandled assertion error instead of returning a page.

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows in OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result() at lines 879-884 that when enable_advanced_features is True and cursor.offset < 0, the code sets start_offset = cursor.offset (a negative value) and then does queryset[start_offset:stop]. Django QuerySets do not support negative indexing - they raise AssertionError or ValueError. The comment claims 'Django ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically' but this is incorrect. This is a real bug that would cause an unhandled exception when this code path is exercised.

adjudication_records.issue_text: src/sentry/api/paginator.py:184 — A negative previous-page offset remains negative in BasePaginator and is passed to a Django QuerySet slice, causing an unhandled assertion error.
matched_golden_ids: In BasePaginator.get_result(), when cursor.is_prev is True, it sets start_offset = offset without clamping, allowing negative offset values to be passed to queryset slicing.
adjudication_records.primary_judge_reasoning: The candidate issue identifies the exact same problem as the golden comment: in BasePaginator, when dealing with a previous page, a negative offset value is not clamped/handled and gets passed to Django QuerySet slicing, which causes an error. Both comments point to the same bug - the lack of clamping for negative offset values when cursor.is_prev is True.

adjudication_records.issue_text: src/sentry/api/paginator.py:838 — The generic paginator hard-codes numeric key conversion even though its only caller supplies a datetime ordering key, leaking cursor value type assumptions across the endpoint boundary.

adjudication.rationale: Looking at line 838 in the diff, the OptimizedCursorPaginator's get_item_key method uses math.floor/math.ceil on the value, which is designed for numeric values. However, the finding claims this is problematic because 'its only caller supplies a datetime ordering key'. Examining the diff, the endpoint passes order_by='-datetime' to the paginator, but this is the ordering field for the queryset, not the key used by get_item_key. The paginator's key attribute (inherited from BasePaginator) would be set separately. The finding makes assumptions about how the paginator is configured that aren't verifiable from the diff. Additionally, the existing DateTimePaginator in the codebase presumably handles datetime keys appropriately, and this new OptimizedCursorPaginator appears to be a separate implementation. The claim about 'leaking cursor value type assumptions' is speculative and not clearly demonstrated by the diff.

adjudication_records.issue_text: src/sentry/api/paginator.py:845 — OptimizedCursorPaginator copies BasePaginator.get_result wholesale instead of isolating its slice policy, creating parallel pagination implementations that must stay synchronized.

adjudication.rationale: The finding correctly identifies that OptimizedCursorPaginator (lines 818-912) duplicates most of the logic from BasePaginator.get_result rather than extending it or isolating just the slice policy difference. Looking at the diff, the new class copies the entire get_result method structure including cursor handling, queryset building, hit counting, and result processing - with only the slice handling being different (lines 875-883). This creates a maintenance burden where changes to BasePaginator.get_result would need to be manually synchronized to OptimizedCursorPaginator. This is a legitimate architectural/scope concern about code duplication introduced by the diff, not a bug but an important design issue.

adjudication_records.issue_text: src/sentry/api/endpoints/organization_auditlogs.py:70 — The optimized_pagination option bypasses AuditLogQueryParamSerializer, splitting query validation and schema ownership between raw request parsing and the serializer.

adjudication.rationale: The finding correctly identifies that the new 'optimized_pagination' query parameter is read directly from request.GET (line 70) rather than being validated through the AuditLogQueryParamSerializer defined at the top of the file. This creates an inconsistency in how query parameters are handled - some go through the serializer (event, actor_id) while this new one bypasses it. This is a legitimate architectural/consistency concern about the diff, though not a bug since the parameter is just a boolean flag that defaults to the safe path when not 'true'.

adjudication_records.issue_text: src/sentry/scripts/spans/add-buffer.lua:63 — ZPOPMIN materializes every evicted payload in the Lua VM even though its result is discarded, causing avoidable Redis memory and CPU spikes on oversized merges

adjudication.rationale: The finding correctly identifies that ZPOPMIN at line 63 returns the evicted elements which are then discarded. Looking at the diff, `redis.call("zpopmin", set_key, span_count - 1000)` is called but its return value is not used. This does cause Redis to serialize and return potentially large payloads unnecessarily. However, this is a performance concern rather than a bug - the code still functions correctly. The finding is valid and specific to the diff, pointing out a real inefficiency that could be addressed by using a different approach (like ZREMRANGEBYRANK) that doesn't return the removed elements.

adjudication_records.issue_text: src/sentry/spans/buffer.py:449 — Removing the span-count cutoff lets oversized or legacy zsets materialize and JSON-decode thousands of tiny spans despite the configured max_segment_spans guard

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows that in buffer.py lines 443-453, the code that previously checked `if len(payloads[key]) > self.max_segment_spans` and would skip/delete oversized segments has been removed. The new code at line 449 just does `payloads[key].extend(span for span, _ in zscan_values)` without any span count limit check. While the Lua script (add-buffer.lua) now enforces a 1000 span limit via `zpopmin`, this is a different limit than `max_segment_spans` which was a configurable Python-side guard. The finding correctly identifies that removing this check allows segments that exceed max_segment_spans to be fully materialized and processed, which could cause performance issues with large/legacy datasets.

adjudication_records.issue_text: src/sentry/spans/buffer.py:197 — Switching live buffer keys from Redis sets to sorted sets without migration makes rolling deploys hit WRONGTYPE and repeatedly fail Kafka processing until legacy keys expire

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows buffer.py changing from Redis set operations (sadd, scard, sscan) to sorted set operations (zadd, zcard, zscan) on the same key pattern 'span-buf:s:{project_and_trace}:{parent_span_id}'. During a rolling deployment, old instances will use set commands while new instances use sorted set commands on the same keys. Redis will return WRONGTYPE errors when a sorted set command is executed on a key that contains a set (or vice versa). This would cause Kafka message processing to fail repeatedly until the old keys expire, which is a real deployment issue.

adjudication_records.issue_text: src/sentry/scripts/spans/add-buffer.lua:47 — ZUNIONSTORE's default SUM makes Kafka replays inflate timestamp scores so eviction can retain replayed old spans and discard newer spans

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows ZUNIONSTORE being used at lines 47 and 52 in add-buffer.lua. ZUNIONSTORE by default uses SUM aggregation for scores. The scores are end_timestamp_precise values (as shown in buffer.py line 196 where zadd uses span.end_timestamp_precise as the score). If the same span payload is processed multiple times (Kafka replay), the scores would be summed, inflating the timestamp. Since zpopmin at line 61 removes spans with the lowest scores (oldest timestamps), inflated scores from replayed spans would cause them to be retained while genuinely newer spans with correct (lower) scores get evicted. This is a real correctness bug.

adjudication_records.issue_text: src/sentry/scripts/spans/add-buffer.lua:30 — Redirect traversal silently stops after 1001 hops without detecting exhaustion so deep traces can be split instead of surfacing a recoverable error

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows the loop limit was reduced from 10000 to 1000 iterations (line 30). The original code had a comment noting 'theoretically this limit means that segment trees of depth 10k may not be joined together correctly.' The finding correctly identifies that when the loop exhausts at 1000 iterations, it silently continues without any error handling or logging - the code just proceeds with whatever set_span_id was found. This is a valid concern about the change: reducing the limit from 10000 to 1000 increases the likelihood of hitting this silent truncation, and there's no mechanism to detect or report when this happens. However, this is not strictly a bug since the original behavior also had this silent truncation issue (just at a higher threshold). It's an important architectural concern about the change making silent data splitting more likely.

adjudication_records.issue_text: src/sentry/api/paginator.py:838 — The optimized audit-log path has no behavioral test, so numeric cursor conversion of its datetime sort key fails on any populated page without detection.

adjudication.rationale: The diff introduces a new OptimizedCursorPaginator class (lines 818-912) that is used for audit log pagination when optimized_pagination=true. The paginator uses get_item_key() which calls math.floor/ceil on the value from getattr(item, self.key). For audit logs, the order_by is '-datetime', meaning the key would be a datetime field. The get_item_key method tries to convert this to int(math.floor(value)), which would fail on datetime objects. The finding correctly identifies that there are no tests for this new paginator with datetime keys - the test files in the diff only update span buffer tests with end_timestamp_precise fields, not pagination tests. This is a legitimate concern about missing test coverage for newly added nontrivial logic.

adjudication_records.issue_text: src/sentry/api/paginator.py:877 — No negative-offset test exercises the advertised advanced path, which passes an invalid negative slice to a Django QuerySet instead of paginating.

adjudication.rationale: The diff introduces a new OptimizedCursorPaginator class with an 'enable_advanced_features' path that allows negative offsets (lines 877-881 in paginator.py). The finding correctly identifies that there are no tests in the diff that exercise this negative offset path. Looking at the test files modified, they only add 'end_timestamp_precise' fields to existing Span objects but don't test the new OptimizedCursorPaginator or its negative offset handling. This is a legitimate concern about missing test coverage for newly added nontrivial logic, though the claim about 'invalid negative slice to Django QuerySet' is somewhat speculative since Django's behavior with negative slices isn't demonstrated in the diff.

adjudication_records.issue_text: src/sentry/scripts/spans/add-buffer.lua:62 — The tests only add identical timestamps to tiny fixtures and never cross the 1,000-span boundary, leaving oldest-first eviction and the exact cap unverified.

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows a new 1000-span cap with zpopmin eviction in add-buffer.lua (lines 55-58), but examining the test files shows all test spans use identical timestamps (1700000000.0) and the test fixtures contain only 4-6 spans each, never approaching the 1000-span limit. This means the oldest-first eviction logic (zpopmin based on end_timestamp_precise scores) is untested. This is a legitimate test coverage gap for newly added functionality.

adjudication_records.issue_text: src/sentry/scripts/spans/add-buffer.lua:62 — No test configures max_segment_spans after enforcement moved to a hard-coded Lua limit, so the existing constructor option can be silently ignored.

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows that the Lua script now enforces a hard-coded limit of 1000 spans (lines 62-64: 'if span_count > 1000 then redis.call("zpopmin", set_key, span_count - 1000)'). Looking at buffer.py, the code that previously checked max_segment_spans in Python (lines 446-452 in the old code) has been removed. The finding correctly identifies that the max_segment_spans constructor option in SpansBuffer could now be silently ignored since enforcement moved to Lua with a hardcoded value. This is a valid concern about configuration options becoming dead code, though the tests do add end_timestamp_precise fields as required by the new schema.

adjudication_records.issue_text: src/sentry/scripts/spans/add-buffer.lua:30 — No boundary test covers the lowered redirect traversal limit at depths 1,000 and 1,001, leaving deep segment joining behavior unverified.

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows the loop limit in add-buffer.lua was changed from 10000 to 1000 (line 30). This is a significant behavioral change that affects how deep segment trees can be joined. The finding correctly identifies that there are no tests in the diff that verify behavior at the new boundary (depths 1000 and 1001). Looking at the test files modified (test_buffer.py, test_flusher.py, test_consumer.py), they only add end_timestamp_precise fields and don't include any tests for deep redirect traversal limits. This is a legitimate concern about missing test coverage for a changed boundary condition.
